# Metadata

As digital objects take shape, they require more than stable [files](glossary.qmd#files) and durable storage. They need structured information that makes them discoverable and intelligible beyond the immediate research context. This is the role of [metadata](glossary.qmd#metadata), which we will explore in this chapter.

## What Is Metadata in Research Data Management?

In the context of Research Data Management, [metadata](glossary.qmd#metadata) is structured information that describes, explains, and contextualises a [digital object](glossary.qmd#digital-object) such as a dataset, document, image, or software file. It acts as a layer of documentation that makes a [digital object](glossary.qmd#digital-object) findable, understandable, and reusable, both now and in the future.

[Metadata](glossary.qmd#metadata) typically captures:

* Content information — what the object contains
* [Provenance](glossary.qmd#provenance) — how, when, and by whom it was created or modified
* Technical characteristics — file formats, structures, and software requirements
* Administrative information — rights, licences, and access conditions
* Relationships — links to other versions, datasets, or publications

In short, metadata provides the context needed to interpret and reuse data beyond its original purpose.

::: {.blank}
:::

## Ontologies, Controlled Vocabularies, Metadata Schemas, and Templates

> **Understanding the Building Blocks of Structured Research Metadata**

In Research Data Management, terms such as *ontologies*, *controlled vocabularies*, *metadata schemas*, and *metadata templates* are often used together. While closely related, they serve distinct roles. Together, they ensure that research outputs are described in a consistent, machine-readable, and interoperable way.

### Controlled Vocabularies

Controlled vocabularies are curated lists of approved terms used to describe data consistently.

They:

* Provide standardised terms for describing concepts
* Reduce ambiguity (e.g., “soil moisture” vs. “soil humidity”)
* Improve searchability and [interoperability](glossary.qmd#interoperability)

#### Examples

* [AGROVOC](https://agrovoc.fao.org/browse/agrovoc/en/) (agriculture)
* [MeSH](https://www.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/meshhome.html) (biomedical terms)
* [GCMD keywords](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/tools/gcmd-keyword-viewer) (Earth science)

When a metadata field requires a *subject keyword*, a controlled vocabulary ensures that everyone uses the same term for the same concept.

Controlled vocabularies give us a shared set of terms. Ontologies build on this foundation by adding structure — showing how those terms relate to one another and how they fit into a broader conceptual model.

##  Ontologies

Ontologies extend controlled vocabularies by not only defining terms, but also specifying the relationships between them.

They:

* Provide a formal, machine-readable model of concepts
* Define hierarchies (e.g., “soil moisture” is a type of “hydrological variable”)
* Enable reasoning and automated linking between datasets

Ontologies often incorporate controlled vocabularies as their lexical foundation, enriching those standardised terms with formal relationships that give them semantic structure.

#### Examples

* [Gene Ontology](https://geneontology.org/docs/ontology-documentation/) (GO)
* [ENVO](https://sites.google.com/site/environmentontology/home) (Environment Ontology)
* [PROV-O](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) (Provenance Ontology)

Ontologies allow machines to understand that terms like “precipitation” and “rainfall” are related, enabling more intelligent search and data integration.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-mesh-vs-do
//| fig-cap: Illustration of how a controlled vocabulary (MeSH) and an ontology (Disease Ontology) represent the same clinical concept, coronary artery disease, using different structural principles. MeSH organises terms in a single‑inheritance hierarchy for indexing, whereas the Disease Ontology models the concept with multiple inheritance and typed relations that capture biological meaning.
//| fig-align: center
//| fig-width: 8
//| output: svg
digraph do_mesh {

    graph [
        rankdir=TB,
        bgcolor="white",
        fontname="Helvetica",
        fontsize=14,
        nodesep=1.0,
        ranksep=1.2
    ];

    node [
        shape=box,
        style="rounded,filled",
        fontname="Helvetica",
        fontsize=14,
        color="#528641",
        fillcolor="#DAEAB4",
        penwidth=2
    ];

    edge [
        fontname="Helvetica",
        fontsize=14,
        color="#528641",
        fontcolor="#528641",
        penwidth=2,
        arrowhead=normal
    ];

    // -------------------------------
    // Disease Ontology (DOID)
    // -------------------------------
    subgraph cluster_DOID {
        label="Disease Ontology (DOID)";
        style="rounded";

        DOID_CVD [label="Cardiovascular system disease"];
        DOID_HD  [label="Heart disease (DOID:114)"];
        DOID_VD  [label="Vascular disease (DOID:178)"];
        DOID_Ath [label="Atherosclerosis (DOID:1936)"];
        DOID_CA  [label="Coronary artery (UBERON:0001621)"];
        DOID_CAD [label="Coronary artery disease (DOID:3393)"];

        // Ontology hierarchy (is_a)
        DOID_CVD -> DOID_HD[label="is_a"];
        DOID_CVD -> DOID_VD[label="is_a"];

        // Ontology logical relations
        DOID_CAD -> DOID_Ath [label="has_material_basis_in", style=dotted];
        DOID_CAD -> DOID_CA  [label="disease_has_location / finding_site", style=dotted];

        // Multiple inheritance example
        DOID_HD -> DOID_CAD[label="is_a"];
        DOID_VD -> DOID_CAD[label="is_a"];
    }

    // -------------------------------
    // MeSH (strict tree)
    // -------------------------------
    subgraph cluster_MeSH {
        label="MeSH";
        style="rounded";

        MeSH_CVD [label="Cardiovascular Diseases (D002318)"];
        MeSH_HD  [label="Heart Diseases (D006331)"];
        MeSH_CAD [label="Coronary Artery Disease (D003324)"];

        // Strict tree structure
        MeSH_CVD -> MeSH_HD;
        MeSH_HD  -> MeSH_CAD;
    }

    // -------------------------------
    // Conceptual alignment
    // -------------------------------
    DOID_CAD -> MeSH_CAD [
        style=dashed,
        label="same clinical concept"
    ];
}
```

@fig-mesh-vs-do highlights how controlled vocabularies and ontologies differ in the way they structure knowledge. In MeSH, “Coronary Artery Disease” appears in a straightforward hierarchical tree under “Heart Diseases,” reflecting its role as a curated list of terms designed for consistent indexing and retrieval. The Disease Ontology, in contrast, represents “Coronary artery disease” as a formal class with multiple parents and additional relations to anatomical and pathological entities. These relations express biological context such as the involvement of the coronary artery or the role of atherosclerosis and support machine‑interpretable reasoning.

Together, these representations show how controlled vocabularies provide stable terminology, while ontologies add semantic structure that enables richer connections between concepts and datasets.

If ontologies describe the meaning of concepts and the relationships between them, metadata schemas address a different question: which pieces of information should be captured when describing a [digital object](glossary.qmd#digital-object).

## Metadata Schemas

A metadata schema defines which fields are used to describe a digital object and how those fields should be structured.

They:

* Specify required and optional fields
* Define field types (e.g. text, date, identifier)
* Ensure consistency across repositories and disciplines

#### Examples

* [Dublin Core](https://www.dcc.ac.uk/resources/metadata-standards/dublin-core) (general-purpose)
* [DataCite](https://schema.datacite.org) (research outputs)
* [DDI](https://ddialliance.org/) (social sciences)
* [CodeMeta](https://codemeta.github.io/terms/) (software)

A metadata schema tells you *what information to provide*, such as:

* Title
* Creator
* Description
* Keywords
* License
* Persistent identifier

Importantly, it does not define which terms to use. That is the role of controlled vocabularies.

Schemas define the structure of metadata, but researchers rarely interact with schemas directly. Templates translate these definitions into practical (web)forms and interfaces that guide real‑world data entry.

## Metadata Templates

A metadata template is a practical, user-friendly implementation of a metadata schema.

They:

* Provide forms or structured documents for data entry
* Translate schema fields into prompts
* Include guidance or examples
* Often embed controlled vocabularies (e.g., dropdowns or autocomplete)

#### Examples

* A Zenodo upload form
* A Dataverse dataset form
* A lab-specific metadata spreadsheet
* A README template aligned with DataCite

Templates are what researchers actually interact with. They operationalise schemas and often help enforce consistency.

These components work together as complementary layers:

| Concept                     | Purpose                  | Relationship                          |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| **Controlled vocabularies** | Standardised terms       | Provide the *values* used in metadata |
| **Ontologies**              | Concepts + relationships | Add semantic meaning and structure    |
| **Metadata schemas**        | Field definitions        | Specify *what* metadata to capture    |
| **Metadata templates**      | Practical tools          | Implement schemas for users           |

##### A simple analogy

* Controlled vocabularies → the dictionary
* Ontologies → the dictionary plus relationships
* Metadata schemas → the blueprint
* Metadata templates → the form you fill in

##### A real-world example

When uploading a dataset to Zenodo:

1. A schema (e.g., DataCite) defines the required fields.
2. The platform presents these fields through a template (web form).
3. Controlled vocabularies may guide keyword selection.
4. Ontologies may link your dataset to related concepts behind the scenes.

Templates shape how metadata is created, but the underlying representation can vary. Some metadata remains simple and tabular, while other forms adopt richer, semantic structures. This leads us to two complementary approaches: key–value metadata and Linked Data.

## Linked Data and Key–Value Metadata

Metadata can range from simple structures to fully semantic representations. Two key approaches are key–value metadata and Linked Data.

### Key–Value Metadata

A common way to record metadata is as a simple list of key–value pairs. It consists of pairs:

* Key → the field name
* Value → the content

#### Examples

* `title: Soil Moisture Dataset 2020–2023`
* `creator: Anna Vermeer`
* `license: CC BY 4.0`

#### Characteristics

* Easy to create and understand
* Common in spreadsheets, JSON, YAML, and repository forms
* Human-readable, but limited in machine interpretation

#### How it fits

* Schemas define the keys
* Controlled vocabularies constrain the values
* Templates present both to the user

Key–value metadata remains the most common way to record basic descriptive information.
It provides a straightforward way to describe digital objects, but it offers limited support for expressing relationships or deeper semantics. Linked Data addresses these limitations by representing information as interconnected statements.

### Linked Data

Linked Data is a more advanced, semantic approach that represents metadata as interconnected statements.
It is most useful when metadata needs to express relationships, connect to external vocabularies, or grow without restructuring. Key–value formats work well for simple descriptions, but Linked Data supports richer semantics, [interoperability](glossary.qmd#interoperability), and long‑term extensibility.
This richer structure allows metadata to be connected across systems, enabling more powerful discovery and integration.

#### Core idea

Information is expressed as subject–predicate–object triples:

* Dataset — *hasCreator* → Anna Vermeer
* Dataset — *hasSubject* → Soil Moisture
* Soil Moisture — *is a* → Hydrological Variable

Each element is identified by a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier), ensuring global uniqueness through a standard web‑style identifier.
In addition to being globally unique, URIs can be looked up, allowing software to retrieve the description of a concept when needed.

##### Characteristics

* Highly interoperable
* Machine-interpretable
* Enables automated reasoning
* Connects datasets across systems

#### How it fits

* Ontologies define relationships
* Controlled vocabularies provide globally unique identifiers for the concepts and terms used
* Schemas can be expressed in machine-readable relationships (triples) using globally unique identifiers
* Templates may generate Linked Data automatically

Linked Data turns metadata into a network of meaning, rather than a collection of fields.

To see how these approaches differ in practice, it helps to compare how they describe the same object using different levels of structure and meaning.


### A Simple Comparison

Describing a book:

* Key–value metadata

  * `title: The Hobbit`
  * `author: J.R.R. Tolkien`

* Controlled vocabulary

  * `subject: Fantasy Fiction`

* Ontology

  * Fantasy Fiction → is a → Fiction Genre

* Schema → defines the fields

* Template → the form

* Linked Data → a connected network (knowledge graph) of relationships

### Key–value pairs versus Linked Data

The table below shows key–value metadata in its familiar tabular form.

| **Field (Key)**  | **Value**                       |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Title            | Soil Moisture Dataset 2020–2023 |
| Creator          | Anna Vermeer, Jeroen de Vries                    |
| Affiliation      | Utrecht University              |
| Publication Year | 2024                            |
| Subject          | Soil moisture                   |
| License          | CC BY 4.0                       |

In this representation:

- Each row stands alone as an independent field–value pair  
- Relationships (e.g., that *Anna Vermeer* and *Jeroen de Vries* are affiliated with *Utrecht University*) are implicit, meaning they are only suggested by the text and not formally expressed in a way that software can interpret  
- Values are plain text, without global identifiers or machine‑interpretable meaning  

When serialised as CSV or TSV, this kind of metadata remains flat and easy to handle, but it cannot express richer structure or semantics.

In @fig-2 below, the *same metadata* is expressed as a small knowledge graph. Instead of isolated fields, we now have entities (dataset, person, organisation, concept) connected by explicit relationships.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-2
//| fig-cap: Knowledge Graph
//| fig-align: center
//| fig-width: 9
//| output: svg

digraph knowledge_graph {

    graph [
        rankdir=TD,
        bgcolor="white",
        fontname="Helvetica",
        fontsize=14,
        nodesep=0.8,
        ranksep=1.0
    ];

    node [
        shape=box,
        style="rounded,filled",
        fontname="Helvetica",
        fontsize=14,
        color="#528641",
        fillcolor="#DAEAB4",
        penwidth=2,
        sketch=1
    ];

    edge [
        fontname="Helvetica",
        fontsize=14,
        color="#528641",
        fontcolor="#528641",
        penwidth=2
    ];

    // Nodes
    D   [label="Dataset"];
    T   [label="Soil Moisture Dataset 2020–2023"];
    Y   [label="2024"];
    L   [label="CC BY 4.0"];
    P1   [label="Person: Anna Vermeer"];
    P2   [label="Person: Jeroen de Vries"];
    S   [label="Concept: Soil Moisture"];
    O   [label="Organisation: Utrecht University"];

    // Edges
    D -> T [label="dc:title"];
    D -> Y [label="dc:issued"];
    D -> L [label="dc:license"];
    D -> P1 [label="dc:creator"];
    D -> P2 [label="dc:creator"];
    D -> S [label="dc:subject"];

    P1 -> O [label="schema:affiliation"];
    P2 -> O [label="schema:affiliation"];
}
```

Compared to the table:

- The table presents metadata as a flat list of fields  
- The graph presents metadata as a network of connected entities  
- The person, organisation, and subject become first‑class nodes  
- Relationships such as `creator` and `affiliation` are explicit and machine‑interpretable

This moves us from *fields with values* to *entities with relationships*.
An RDF graph — the Resource Description Framework — represents metadata as a network of interconnected entities, where each connection is expressed as a triple linking a subject, predicate, and object. Once metadata is expressed in this way, it can be serialised using a Linked Data format such as Turtle.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

### The knowledge graph above written down in Turtle. 

```turtle
@prefix dc:     <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/> .
@prefix dct:    <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> .
@prefix schema: <http://schema.org/> .
@prefix foaf:   <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> .
@prefix skos:   <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#> .
@prefix rdfs:   <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix xsd:    <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

# Dataset node (using schema:Dataset)
<https://data.example.org/dataset/soil-moisture-2020-2023>
    a schema:Dataset ;
    dc:title "Soil Moisture Dataset 2020–2023" ;
    dct:issued "2024"^^xsd:gYear ;
    dct:license <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/> ;
    dct:creator <https://data.example.org/person/anna-vermeer> ;
    dct:subject <https://vocab.example.org/concept/soil-moisture> .

# Person node (FOAF)
<https://data.example.org/person/anna-vermeer>
    a foaf:Person ;
    foaf:name "Anna Vermeer" ;
    foaf:member <https://data.example.org/org/utrecht-university> .

# Organisation node (FOAF)
<https://data.example.org/org/utrecht-university>
    a foaf:Organization ;
    foaf:name "Utrecht University" .

# Concept node (SKOS)
<https://vocab.example.org/concept/soil-moisture>
    a skos:Concept ;
    skos:prefLabel "Soil Moisture"@en ;
    skos:definition "The amount of water contained in soil, typically expressed as a percentage."@en .
```

:::

In this serialisation, the RDF graph not only describes the dataset, the creator, and the organisation, but also provides a stable identifier for the subject concept (“Soil Moisture”). This makes the metadata interoperable: other datasets can refer to the same concept, and machines can follow the URI to retrieve its meaning.

The prefixes at the top of the file indicate which vocabularies and ontologies the graph draws on, allowing each property and class to be referenced unambiguously. For example:

```
@prefix dc:     <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/> .
```

This prefix simply states that `dc:title` refers to the full URI <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/title>,  
the authoritative definition of the Dublin Core `title` property.

By giving each entity, i.e. dataset, person, organisation and concept its own URI, the graph becomes a reusable and extensible structure. Machines can infer relationships, merge graphs, or enrich them with external knowledge. While it is technically possible to use URIs as keys in key–value metadata, such formats lack the semantics and inference capabilities that RDF provides.

We explore metadata serialisation and metadata infrastructure in more detail in the chapter [Metadata Infrastructure](metadata-infrastructure.qmd).

## Bringing It All Together

The layers described above build on one another, moving from simple descriptions to richer semantic structures. Seeing how they connect helps clarify how different metadata standards work together in practice.

* Key–value metadata is the practical starting point
* Linked Data is the semantic, interoperable extension
* Controlled vocabularies and ontologies provide meaning and standardisation of terms
* Schemas and templates provide structure

Together, these elements give us a coherent picture of how metadata can be structured and enriched. With this broader view in place, we can look more closely at specific metadata standards and how they complement one another across different domains.

## Understanding and Combining Metadata Standards

Metadata standards vary in scope—from general to highly specialised. Understanding how they complement each other helps in selecting the right approach.

### Dublin Core

A general-purpose, lightweight metadata schema.

It provides:

* 15 core elements (e.g., Title, Creator, Subject, Date)
* Broad applicability across domains

Why it’s useful:

* Simple and widely supported
* Suitable for discovery and basic description

Role: Provides baseline descriptive metadata.

### PROV-O

A provenance ontology describing how data was created.

It provides

* Entities, activities, and agents
* Relationships such as `wasGeneratedBy` and `used`

Why it’s useful:

* Supports reproducibility
* Captures workflows and processes

Role: Adds semantic provenance and process context.


### Discipline-Specific Schema - ␀37␀

Data Documentation Initiative (DDI) organises metadata into three main levels:

| Level              | What it describes            | Examples                                    |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| **Study level**    | The overall research project | Title, investigators, methodology, sampling |
| **Dataset level**  | The data [files](glossary.qmd#files)               | File format, number of variables, version   |
| **Variable level** | Individual variables         | Question text, response categories, coding  |

The **variable level** is what makes DDI especially powerful.

Study level

* Title: European Social Survey 2022
* Method: Survey
* Sample: Random sample of EU residents

Dataset level

* File: `ess2022.csv`
* Cases: 30,000 respondents
* Variables: 250

Variable level

* Variable: `trust_gov`
* Question: “How much do you trust the national government?”
* Values:

  * 0 = No trust
  * 10 = Complete trust

DDI enables researchers to understand:

* what the data contains (variables),
* how it was collected (methodology), and
* how to reuse it correctly.

It provides:

* Detailed methodological and variable-level metadata
* Support for complex datasets

Why it’s useful:

* Captures domain knowledge essential for reuse

Role: Provides deep, field-specific context.

### Discipline-Specific Schema - Investigation–Study–Assay (ISA)

[ISA](https://isa-specs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) is a discipline-specific metadata framework used in the life sciences to describe experimental workflows, especially in genomics, proteomics, and other omics research.

ISA organises metadata into three hierarchical levels:

| Level             | What it describes                        | Examples                                       |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| **Investigation** | The overall research context             | Project title, researchers, objectives         |
| **Study**         | A specific experiment or dataset         | Study design, subjects, sample characteristics |
| **Assay**         | Analytical measurements and technologies | Sequencing, mass spectrometry, protocols       |

The assay level captures how data was actually generated.

Investigation level

* Title: Gut Microbiome and Diet Study
* Objective: Analyse microbiome changes under different diets

Study level

* Subjects: 100 participants
* Design: Controlled dietary intervention
* Samples: Stool samples collected weekly

Assay level

* Technology: DNA sequencing
* Platform: Illumina
* Output: Microbial abundance profiles

ISA enables researchers to understand:

* what was studied (samples and subjects),
* how experiments were conducted, and
* how measurements were generated.

It provides:

* Detailed methodological and variable-level metadata
* Support for complex datasets

Why it’s useful:

* Captures domain knowledge essential for reuse

Role: Provides deep, field-specific context.


### How They Work Together

| Layer               | Purpose                       | Example                                    |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| General description | What is it?                   | Dublin Core                                |
| Provenance          | How was it created?           | PROV-O                                     |
| Domain detail       | What does it mean in context? | DDI (social sciences), ISA (life sciences) |

Together, these layers create rich, [FAIR](glossary.qmd#fair), and interoperable metadata. With them in place, metadata becomes both meaningful within its discipline and interoperable across the wider research landscape.

In this chapter we introduced URIs as globally unique identifiers for concepts, properties, and relationships within semantic metadata. These identifiers help machines understand what a term refers to and how different entities are connected.
To make research objects themselves—datasets, software, publications, instruments, samples—equally stable and unambiguous, we need identifiers that serve the same purpose at the data object level and remain reliable over time, even as locations or infrastructures change.
This is the role of Persistent Identifiers. They apply the principle of stable, globally unique identification to the objects that metadata describes, ensuring that those objects can be cited, discovered, and linked long after their storage or access conditions evolve.
